about: Overview

Leaflegal is free for people and businesses to use. You do not pay us to fill in the form, to be introduced to a firm or at any point afterwards. We are paid by the law firms we introduce people to. This page explains exactly how that works and what it means for you.

We think you have a right to know how a service like ours is funded before you use it. Many websites that help people find lawyers are not clear about this. Some do not say who runs them. Some send your details to several firms and are paid by each one. We would rather tell you plainly, so you can decide for yourself whether you are comfortable using us.

about: Leaflegal is a trading name of Vertical Brands Ltd, a company registered in England and Wales with company number 14254961. We are an introduction service. We are not a law firm, we do not give legal advice or immigration advice, and we are not regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority.
The firms we introduce are independent and regulated for the work they do. They are separate businesses from Leaflegal, and they are responsible for the advice and service they give you.

When you look for a lawyer, you are often doing so at a difficult time. You need to be able to trust the people helping you take that first step. Being clear about money is a big part of that trust. If you understand who is paying whom and why, you can weigh up what you hear and make your own decisions with confidence.

It also helps to know what the introduction fee does not do. It does not buy the firm a guarantee that you will instruct it. It does not buy influence over the advice the firm gives. And it does not give anyone else access to the details of your matter.
Who pays
Every business has to pay for itself somehow. For Leaflegal, the money comes from the law firms that receive introductions from us.

Firms that want to receive enquiries from Leaflegal agree terms with us in writing. They choose which areas of law, types of matter and locations they handle. When we introduce an enquiry to a firm, the firm pays us an agreed fee for that introduction. The amount is agreed individually with each firm.
The fee is for the introduction itself. It is not linked to whether you go on to instruct the firm, how much the firm earns from your matter or the outcome of your case.

The income from firms covers the cost of running Leaflegal. That includes building and maintaining the website and the form, our advertising, the checks we carry out on each enquiry, keeping records of consent, handling questions and complaints, and writing and updating the guides on our website.

about.h3: Why firms are willing to pay

about: Firms spend money on finding new clients in many ways, such as advertising online, paying for directory listings, running their own websites and sponsoring local events. Paying for an introduction is another way of doing the same thing. For the firm, the advantage is that it hears from people who have already said what kind of help they need and have asked to be contacted.
Nothing to us. If you decide to instruct the firm, you pay the firm for its legal work on the terms you agree with it. That is the same as if you had found the firm in any other way.

Firms pay for each introduction they receive, rather than paying for a listing or for a share of their fees. That keeps the arrangement simple. It also means our income depends on making introductions that firms find genuinely useful, which in turn depends on people being introduced to the right kind of firm for their matter.

Sometimes an enquiry turns out to be something a firm cannot help with, for example because the details given were wrong or the matter is outside the area it covers. Our written agreements with firms deal with situations like this. None of that affects you, and you are never asked to pay anything.
What it means for you
Knowing that the firm pays us, it is natural to wonder whether that affects you. Here is how we keep the arrangement fair.

about.h3: Your bill does not go up

about: The fee the firm pays us does not change what the firm charges you. The firm sets its own prices and will explain them to you on the first call. It will confirm them in writing before any work starts. You are free to compare those prices with other firms.

Each enquiry goes to one firm only. We do not sell your enquiry to several firms or run an auction for it. That means you are not chased by lots of firms at once, and the firm that contacts you knows it is the only one introduced to you through us.

There is no obligation to instruct the firm we introduce. You can ask questions, take time to think, speak to other firms and choose whoever you prefer. Using Leaflegal does not commit you to anything.

The firm's lawyers are responsible for the advice they give you, and they owe you professional duties as their client. Their regulators expect them to act in your best interests and not to let a referral arrangement affect their advice.

If you want to know more about the introduction fee, you can ask the firm, and you can ask us. We will explain how the arrangement works. We do not publish the individual amounts agreed with firms because they are commercial arrangements, but we are always happy to explain the principles.

about.h3: Comparing with other ways of finding a lawyer

about: Whatever route you take to find a lawyer, someone usually pays for the firm to reach you. Search engines are paid for adverts, directories are paid for listings and some websites are paid for each enquiry. The difference with Leaflegal is that we tell you about it openly, we only send your enquiry to one firm and the firm must tell you about the fee in writing.
The rules
Introductions from services like Leaflegal to law firms are allowed, but they are subject to rules. Those rules are there to protect you.

Solicitors regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority must tell clients in writing when a client has been introduced through an arrangement where the firm pays a fee. That information is usually included in the firm's client care letter or terms of business. It means the arrangement is never hidden from you.

The same rules say that a referral arrangement must not affect the firm's independence or the advice it gives. The firm must act in your best interests. If you feel that is not happening, you can raise it with the firm, and concerns about a solicitor's conduct can be reported to the SRA.

about.h3: Areas where referral fees are banned

about: In some areas of law, referral fees are not allowed at all. The best known are personal injury and clinical negligence claims. Leaflegal does not cover those areas, and we do not take payments for introductions in them. We also do not cover housing disrepair or financial mis-selling claims.

Licensed conveyancers and regulated immigration advisers have their own regulators and their own rules on introductions and transparency. Whichever kind of firm you are introduced to, it should explain its fees clearly and be open with you about how it came to have your details.

As a company we must follow UK law, including data protection and consumer protection law. That means being clear about who we are, only sharing your details with your consent and not misleading you about what we do. We take those obligations seriously and we explain them on our website.

Before we pass your enquiry to a firm, you agree on the form to be introduced and contacted. We record the wording you agreed to and when you agreed, and we send that record with your enquiry. It means the firm can see that you asked to hear from it, and it means there is a clear record if anyone ever needs to check.
Keeping it fair
An arrangement where firms pay for introductions only works if people can trust it. These are the principles we follow.

We introduce each enquiry to a firm because it handles that type of matter and covers your area. We do not send your enquiry to whichever firm pays us most at that moment, and we do not rank firms by what they pay.

We do not tell you that a firm will win your case, get you a particular result or finish by a certain date. Every matter depends on its own facts. We also do not publish testimonials or success rates, because they can give a misleading impression of what will happen in your case.

We only introduce firms that are regulated for the work they do. That gives you the protections that come with a regulated firm, such as professional indemnity insurance, a complaints procedure and access to the Legal Ombudsman for service complaints.
If a firm does not treat someone fairly, we want to know. We may stop working with firms that do not meet the standards we expect. Telling us helps protect the next person who uses Leaflegal.

about.h3: Your information is not for sale

about: We share your enquiry with the one firm we introduce, and only because you agreed. We never share the details of your matter with advertisers or data brokers, and we do not sell your details to lists of firms.

We would rather introduce fewer people well than many people badly. If an enquiry is clearly outside the areas we cover, we do not pass it to a firm just because a fee would be paid. If we are unsure, we check first. Firms rely on us to send them people they can genuinely help, and people rely on us to send them to firms that do their kind of work.
Questions to ask

Whether you found a firm through Leaflegal or another way, it is worth understanding how it charges and how it found you. These questions can help on the first call or once you receive the firm's terms of business.

list: Is your fee fixed, or charged by the hour
What exactly does the fee include
What disbursements are likely, such as court, search or registration fees
Is VAT included in the figures you have given me
When will you ask me to pay, and how much up front
What could make the cost go up, and will you tell me before it does
How did you receive my details
Do you pay a fee for introductions, and where is that set out
Does the introduction affect what you charge me

about: The firm's client care letter and terms of business should cover most of these points. If something is not clear, ask the firm to explain it before you agree to go ahead. For questions about Leaflegal's part in the arrangement, you can email us at any time.

Read the firm's terms of business carefully. Check the fee, the disbursements, the payment terms and how the firm will tell you if the cost estimate changes. Look for the section about how you were introduced. If anything is missing or unclear, ask the firm to explain or to put it in writing before you agree.
faqs: Paying for Leaflegal
Is Leaflegal really free?

Yes. There is no charge to fill in the form, no charge to be introduced and no charge afterwards. We are paid by the firm we introduce you to. You will never receive a bill from Leaflegal, and you are under no obligation to instruct the firm.
Will I be asked for card details?

No. Leaflegal never asks you for card or bank details. If anyone claiming to be from Leaflegal asks you for payment, do not pay and contact us. If you instruct a firm, the firm will explain how to pay its own fees in its terms of business.
Is there a catch?

We do not think so. The firm pays for the introduction, you get a free and focused introduction to a firm that handles your type of matter, and you decide whether to go ahead. We explain the arrangement on this page so that you can judge for yourself.
Do I pay anything if I do not go ahead?

No. If you speak to the firm and decide not to instruct it, you owe nothing to Leaflegal and nothing to the firm, unless you have separately agreed to pay the firm for a consultation. The firm will always tell you before any charge applies.
Why don't you charge clients?

Because we think the first step towards legal help should be free and easy. Many people put off speaking to a lawyer because they worry about cost. Keeping Leaflegal free removes one barrier, and the firm then explains its own fees clearly so you can decide.
Will Leaflegal ever start charging me?

Leaflegal is designed to be free for people and businesses looking for legal help. If that ever changed, we would make it very clear on the website before you used the service, and you would never be charged for an introduction you had already received.
Is VAT charged on Leaflegal's service?

No, because you do not pay Leaflegal anything. VAT may apply to the firm's own legal fees if you instruct it. Ask the firm whether the figures it gives you include VAT, so that you can compare quotes on a like for like basis.
The fee firms pay
How much does the firm pay you?

The fee is agreed individually with each firm as a commercial arrangement, so we do not publish the amounts. What matters for you is that the fee does not change what the firm charges you and that solicitors must tell you about it in writing.
Is the fee added to my legal bill?

No. The firm sets its own prices and they are the same whether or not you were introduced by Leaflegal. The fee the firm pays us comes out of the firm's own marketing budget, in the same way as its spending on advertising or directory listings.
Does the firm pay more if it wins my case?

No. The fee is for the introduction only. It is not linked to whether you instruct the firm, how much the firm earns from your matter or the result. That means we have no interest in pushing you towards a particular decision.
Does the firm pay if I decide not to instruct it?

Yes. Firms pay for the introduction itself, whether or not the person goes on to instruct them. That is part of what keeps the arrangement fair. Leaflegal does not gain anything from you choosing one way or the other.
Do firms pay to appear higher on your website?
No. Leaflegal does not list or rank firms, and firms cannot pay to be shown to you ahead of others. We introduce each enquiry to one firm that handles that type of matter and covers your area.
Do you take payments from anyone else?

Our income comes from the firms that receive introductions from us. We do not take payments from advertisers in return for sharing the details of your matter, and we do not sell your information to data brokers or other companies.
Do firms sign an agreement with you?

Yes. Every firm that receives introductions from Leaflegal agrees terms with us in writing. Those terms cover things like pricing, billing, how enquiries are delivered and what happens if an enquiry turns out to be invalid. They do not give the firm any say over the advice it gives you.
Fairness and advice
Does the fee affect the advice I get?

It must not. Solicitors must act in their clients' best interests, and the rules say a referral arrangement must not affect their independence or the advice they give. The firm's lawyers are responsible for their advice to you and accountable to their regulator.
How do I know the firm is right for me?

Ask the firm about its experience with matters like yours, who will do the work and how it charges. You can check a solicitor on the SRA register. If you are not comfortable, you are free to speak to other firms before deciding. There is no obligation to go ahead.
Do you choose the firm that pays you most?

No. We introduce each enquiry based on the type of matter and your location. We do not auction enquiries or send them to whichever firm is paying most. Each enquiry goes to one firm only and is not passed on to anyone else.
Why don't you cover personal injury?

Referral fees are banned for personal injury and clinical negligence claims. Because Leaflegal is funded by firms paying for introductions, we do not cover those areas. We also do not cover housing disrepair or financial mis-selling claims.
Can Leaflegal tell me if the firm's quote is fair?

No. We do not give legal advice and we do not assess firms' prices. If you want to compare, you can ask other firms for a quote. When you compare, check that each quote includes the same things, such as disbursements and VAT.
What if I think a firm has not been open with me?

Raise it with the firm first, because every regulated firm must have a complaints procedure. Please tell us as well. If the firm does not resolve a service complaint within eight weeks, you may be able to go to the Legal Ombudsman. Conduct concerns can go to the SRA.
Will the firm try to sell me extra services?

A regulated firm should only recommend work that is in your interests. It may mention related matters, such as a will when you buy a home, because they are often relevant. You are free to say no. If you feel pressured, raise it with the firm and let us know.
Can I use Leaflegal and still shop around?

Yes. Many people speak to the firm we introduce and also ask one or two other firms for a quote. That is completely fine. There is no exclusivity on your side, and nothing in our arrangement with the firm stops you choosing someone else.
Transparency
Where will the firm tell me about the fee?

Usually in its client care letter or terms of business, which it sends before any work starts. If you cannot find it, ask the firm to point it out. Solicitors must tell you in writing, so it should be easy to find.
Why do you explain all this?

Because we think you should know how a service is paid for before you use it. Being open about money helps you make an informed choice and makes it easier to trust the introduction. If anything on this page is unclear, email us and we will explain.
Is Leaflegal a law firm?

No. Leaflegal is an introduction service and a trading name of Vertical Brands Ltd. We are not a law firm, we do not give legal advice or immigration advice, and we are not regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority. The firm you are introduced to gives the advice.
Do you share my details with the firm for free?

We share your details with one firm, and only because you agreed to it on the form. The firm pays us for the introduction. We record the consent you gave and send it with your enquiry so that it is clear you asked to be contacted.
Who can I ask about this page?

Email us and a member of our team will reply. We are happy to explain how introductions work, what firms agree to and how we handle your information. We cannot discuss the legal side of your matter, which is a question for the firm.
Do you publish a list of the firms you work with?

No. We introduce each enquiry to a firm that handles that kind of matter and covers your area, and the firm identifies itself when it contacts you. You can then check the firm's regulation and reputation for yourself before you decide whether to go ahead.
Can a firm ask you not to tell me about the fee?

No. Being open about the introduction is part of how we work, and solicitors must tell clients about referral fees in writing. We explain the arrangement on our website for everyone to read, and we would not work with a firm that wanted it hidden.
Immigration introductions
Does the same arrangement apply to immigration?

Yes. For immigration we introduce you to a regulated immigration adviser, who pays us for the introduction in the same way. Leaflegal does not give immigration advice or provide immigration services. The adviser will explain their own fees and how they work before you agree to anything.
Who regulates immigration advisers?

Immigration advice in the UK can only be given by people who are regulated to do so. That includes solicitors regulated by the SRA, barristers and advisers registered with the Immigration Advice Authority. You can ask the adviser who regulates them and check their registration.
Will the adviser charge me for the first call?

The adviser will explain how they charge. Some offer a short initial call at no cost, while others charge a fixed fee for a full consultation. They should tell you before any charge applies, and confirm their fees in writing before starting work.
Can Leaflegal tell me whether I need an adviser?

No. Leaflegal does not give immigration advice and cannot comment on your situation. If you are unsure, the adviser we introduce can talk it through with you on the first call and explain how they could help, if at all.
Is the referral fee mentioned by immigration advisers too?

Immigration advisers have their own regulators and rules. Whatever their regulator, the adviser should be open with you about its fees and about how it came to have your details. If you are unsure, ask the adviser to explain the arrangement and to set it out in writing.
